concepts.decision: Write each requirement with context, owner, measurable acceptance evidence, and any approved exception before selecting implementation.
concepts.definition: Observable security outcomes or constraints the system must satisfy, such as authorized access, integrity protection, auditable events, or safe failure.
concepts.failureExample: “Use encryption” without scope, key authority, and a test leaves confidentiality behavior ambiguous.
concepts.label: Security Requirements

concepts.decision: Identify data purpose and lifecycle with privacy stakeholders, then define constraints and evidence for the affected flow.
concepts.definition: Requirements governing lawful and appropriate collection, use, disclosure, retention, access, and deletion of personal data in the product.
concepts.failureExample: A feature can meet functional needs while retaining personal data longer or sharing it more broadly than allowed.
concepts.label: Privacy Requirements

concepts.decision: Perform and update it when architecture, data flow, exposure, or key assumptions change; use results to choose controls and tests.
concepts.definition: Structured analysis of assets, actors, trust boundaries, entry points, abuse cases, and control assumptions from an attacker perspective.
concepts.failureExample: Reusing a model after adding an external queue misses the new boundary and abuse paths.
concepts.label: Threat Modeling

concepts.decision: Choose a control because it mitigates a modeled abuse case and document its dependencies, failure behavior, and verification.
concepts.definition: Architecture and detailed design that deliberately enforces requirements through boundaries, authorization, validation, isolation, cryptography, logging, and resilient behavior.
concepts.failureExample: Adding authentication without authorization can still let a valid low-privilege user initiate refunds.
concepts.label: Secure Design

concepts.decision: Use the IPT early to resolve conflicting requirements and assign owners for decisions that cross disciplines.
concepts.definition: A cross-functional group that makes product tradeoffs with product, engineering, security, privacy, operations, legal, and relevant users/partners.
concepts.failureExample: A security team discovering a retention constraint after release may require costly redesign or unlawful processing.
concepts.label: Integrated Product Team

concepts.decision: Make criteria trace to the requirement and abuse case; test normal, failure, and misuse behavior before acceptance or explicit risk disposition.
concepts.definition: Pre-agreed, observable conditions and evidence used to decide whether a delivered system meets its specified requirements.
concepts.failureExample: A login test that proves only a valid user can sign in does not prove invalid signatures or unauthorized roles are rejected.
concepts.label: Acceptance Criteria

misconceptions.claim: A security review at the end can recover missed requirements cheaply.
misconceptions.correction: Late discovery can require architectural change; early traceable requirements reduce rework while operation still needs monitoring.

outcome: Translate stakeholder risk into testable requirements and threat-informed design decisions.

sections.body: An Integrated Product Team brings product, engineering, security, privacy, operations, legal, and user representatives into requirements and tradeoffs. Express confidentiality, integrity, availability, privacy, resilience, abuse prevention, logging, and recovery needs as observable acceptance criteria with owners and exceptions.
keyPoints: Security and privacy requirements should be testable rather than slogans.
IPT participation exposes dependency and operational constraints early.
Trace each material requirement to design, test evidence, and risk acceptance.
sections.title: Make security a shared product decision

sections.body: Threat modeling identifies assets, actors, trust boundaries, entry points, misuse cases, and control assumptions. Use the result to choose authentication, authorization, input handling, isolation, encryption, logging, and resilience controls; record assumptions and revisit them when architecture or data flows change.
keyPoints: A threat model is a decision aid, not a one-time document.
Security design must include service dependencies and operational paths.
Acceptance criteria should prove the control works against the modeled abuse case.
sections.title: Design from abuse paths and boundaries

workedExamples.reasoning: The IPT identifies the new partner-to-service trust boundary, spoofing and replay abuse cases, and personal-data flow. It writes the requirement “Only authenticated partner messages with a fresh, unique request identifier may initiate a refund; rejected messages create an audit event without exposing payment data.” Design selects signature validation, nonce storage, authorization, rate limiting, and safe logs. Acceptance evidence includes replay, invalid-signature, and authorization tests plus the named product owner’s exception decision.
